slides.title: A tensor is an array with a shape, a number format and a device
slides.text: What a tensor is A tensor is an array with a shape, a number format and a device Shape : how many axes, how long each one is Number format : 32-bit floats by default; 64-bit when you check arithmetic Device : the processor or a graphics processor; two tensors must share one One more thing than an array: it can remember how it was computed X.shape # torch.Size([4, 576]) X.dtype # torch.float32 X.device # cpu W1.requires_grad # True At Al-Nawl. A batch of four grey swatches of 24 by 24 pixels is a tensor of shape (4, 576).

slides.title: Eight patterns, laid straight on the sorting table
slides.text: Today's data Eight patterns, laid straight on the sorting table 4,000 synthetic swatches: 3,000 to train, 500 to validate, 500 to test. Grey, 24 by 24 pixels, 576 numbers each.

slides.title: Predict the shape before you run the line
slides.text: Shapes Predict the shape before you run the line Operation Shapes in Shape out X @ W1 (4, 576) and (576, 5) (4, 5) X @ W1 + b1 (4, 5) and (5,) (4, 5) X.mean(axis=0) (4, 576) (576,) X.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True) (4, 576) (4, 1) X - X.mean(axis=1) (4, 576) and (4,) an error What goes wrong. Most deep learning bugs are shape bugs that do not raise an error: a shape of (4,) against (4, 1) broadcasts to (4, 4) and trains on nonsense.

slides.title: Shapes align from the right; a size of 1 stretches
slides.text: Broadcasting Shapes align from the right; a size of 1 stretches Works (4, 576) with (576,): the last axes match, the vector is repeated over the 4 rows. (4, 576) with (4, 1): the 1 stretches over the 576 columns. Fails, or worse (4, 576) with (4,): 576 against 4, an error. (4,) with (4, 1): no error, a (4, 4) table nobody asked for. Habit. Print .shape after every new line until the shapes are boring.

slides.title: Two layers: multiply, bend, multiply, compare
slides.text: The network of today Two layers: multiply, bend, multiply, compare Input X: (N, 576) → Layer 1 z1 = X W1 + b1, then relu → Layer 2 z2 = h W2 + b2: eight scores → Loss softmax, then −log p of the true class The eight raw scores are called logits; softmax turns them into probabilities Cross-entropy is the mean of −log p(true class): 0 when certain and right, ln 8 = 2.08 when guessing among eight

slides.title: The backward pass is the chain rule, one local step at a time
slides.text: Gradients The backward pass is the chain rule, one local step at a time Softmax with cross-entropy: dz2 = (p − onehot) / N Linear layer: dW = a.T @ dz, db = dz.sum(0) Pass back: da = dz @ W.T Relu: the gradient passes where z1 > 0 One rule to check everything A gradient has the shape of the thing it is the gradient of. dW1 is (576, 5) because W1 is. You know this. It is the chain rule of FN-103, written for matrices. The lab does it for four swatches.

slides.title: The library records the forward pass and replays it backwards
slides.text: Automatic differentiation The library records the forward pass and replays it backwards W1 = torch.tensor(w1, requires_grad=True) z2 = torch.relu(X @ W1 + b1) @ W2 + b2 loss = F.cross_entropy(z2, y) loss.backward() W1.grad.shape # (576, 5) Each operation adds a node to a computational graph backward() applies the local rules from the loss to every leaf Gradients add up in .grad until you clear them 1e-16 largest gap between hand and autograd in Lab 1.1, in 64-bit numbers; 9e-8 between a 32-bit and a 64-bit run

slides.title: Which gradient is right?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which gradient is right? A layer computes z = a @ W + b with a of shape (32, 64) and W of shape (64, 8). You have dz, the gradient of the loss with respect to z. Which line gives the gradient for W? dz @ W.T a @ dz a.T @ dz dz.sum(axis=0)

slides.text: Session 2 Writing the training loop Write a training step: forward, loss, backward, update Draw mini-batches from a shuffled training set Measure validation loss and accuracy without gradients 02

slides.title: Every training step is the same five lines
slides.text: The training step Every training step is the same five lines logits = model(xb) # 1 forward loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, yb) # 2 loss optimiser.zero_grad() # 3 clear old gradients loss.backward() # 4 backward optimiser.step() # 5 update the weights From a two-layer network to a language model , these five lines do not change. What changes is the model, the data and the loss.

slides.title: Cross-entropy takes logits, not probabilities
slides.text: The loss Cross-entropy takes logits, not probabilities F.cross_entropy applies the softmax itself, in a numerically safe way Its inputs: raw scores of shape (N, classes) and class numbers of shape (N,) Give it probabilities and it applies a second softmax: no error, a loss that cannot reach zero 1.27 the loss of a perfect prediction when softmax is applied twice (Lab 1.4)

slides.title: The optimiser is the rule that turns a gradient into a step
slides.text: The optimiser The optimiser is the rule that turns a gradient into a step Gradient descent (SGD) w = w − lr × grad. One setting: the learning rate is the step size and nothing else. Adam Keeps a running average of each weight's gradient and of its square, and scales every step by them. Forgiving: a rate of 0.001 works on most small problems. In the labs. Adam when the point is the loop (1.2), plain gradient descent when the point is the learning rate (1.3, 1.4).

slides.title: A mini-batch is a noisy, cheap estimate of the full gradient
slides.text: Batches A mini-batch is a noisy, cheap estimate of the full gradient All 3,000 swatches per step: an exact gradient, one update per pass 32 swatches per step: a noisy gradient, 94 updates per pass An epoch is one pass over the training set in a new random order Shuffle every epoch, and keep each input with its own label What goes wrong. Inputs shuffled without their labels give a network nothing to learn.

slides.title: The validation pass measures and must not learn
slides.text: Validation The validation pass measures and must not learn model.eval() with torch.no_grad(): logits = model(Xva) loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, yva) acc = (logits.argmax(1) == yva) .float().mean() eval(): layers that behave differently in training switch to their test behaviour no_grad(): no graph is recorded, so no memory and no time are spent on it Once per epoch, on data the training step never sees

slides.title: Both losses fall together, from chance towards zero
slides.text: What a healthy run looks like Both losses fall together, from chance towards zero 0.79 validation accuracy after 12 epochs; chance is 0.125 37,448 weights, Adam at 0.001, batches of 32. Validation loss from 1.99 to 0.70 (Lab 1.2, reference run).

slides.title: Two correct runs differ; say by how much they may
slides.text: Reproducibility Two correct runs differ; say by how much they may A different batch order or seed gives a different path to a similar place Fix the seed to repeat your run; state a tolerance to compare with someone else's Keep the curve as a file, with the settings that produced it Experiment tracking (MLflow, TensorBoard) is this habit with a user interface: one record per run with its settings, its curves and its code version.

slides.title: The curve that jumps
slides.text: Checkpoint The curve that jumps Zaid's loop runs. The training loss falls for a few steps, then swings wildly and grows. His step has four lines: forward, loss, loss.backward(), optimiser.step(). What is the most likely cause? Gradients from earlier steps are still added to each new one The model was never put in evaluation mode The batches were not shuffled between epochs The batch size of 32 is too small for this network

slides.title: Tune the learning rate first: it decides whether anything else matters
slides.text: The learning rate Tune the learning rate first: it decides whether anything else matters 0.001 : flat at 2.08, accuracy 0.11. Too low: the weights barely move 0.1 : falls to 1.23, accuracy 0.62. Usable 3.0 : between 2.4 and 12. Too high: every step overshoots

slides.title: Sweep powers of ten, read curves, then refine
slides.text: How to search Sweep powers of ten, read curves, then refine 1 · Coarse 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1: a few epochs each → 2 · Read too low, usable or too high, from the validation curve → 3 · Refine two or three values around the best one Change one setting at a time, from the same starting weights A larger batch gives a less noisy gradient and usually tolerates a larger rate Schedules (warm-up, decay) shape the rate over time; a constant rate is the baseline

slides.title: The gap between the two losses is what the network memorised
slides.text: Overfitting The gap between the two losses is what the network memorised Training loss keeps falling as long as the network has capacity to spare Validation loss stops falling when the rest is particular to the training examples The gap grows with a larger network, a smaller training set, more epochs At Al-Nawl. With 400 swatches and 256 hidden units: training loss 0.52, validation loss 0.95 after 60 epochs. A gap of 0.43 (Lab 1.3).

slides.title: Dropout and weight decay make memorising harder
slides.text: Regularisation Dropout and weight decay make memorising harder Dropout In training, each hidden unit is switched off with probability p at every step. No unit can rely on one other unit. Off in evaluation mode. Weight decay Every step also pulls each weight a little towards zero. Large weights must earn their size. Augmentation Show changed copies that keep the label: a flipped or shifted image. More data without new labels. Day 2. What goes wrong. Validating with dropout still on: the model is measured with half its units missing. This is what model.eval() prevents.

slides.title: The gap shrank; the validation loss hardly moved
slides.text: What the lab measured The gap shrank; the validation loss hardly moved 400 swatches, 60 epochs Training loss Validation loss Gap Validation accuracy Plain 0.52 0.95 0.43 0.64 Dropout 0.5 0.86 1.05 0.19 0.68 Weight decay 0.001 0.60 0.93 0.33 0.64 All 3,000 swatches, 12 epochs (Lab 1.2) 0.73 0.70 0 0.79 Read it honestly. Regularisation stops a network from flattering itself. It does not replace the data that is missing.

slides.title: Keep the weights of the best validation epoch
slides.text: When to stop Keep the weights of the best validation epoch Watch the validation loss; save the weights whenever it improves Patience : stop after this many epochs without an improvement A noisy curve needs more patience: with 500 validation swatches, a patience of 3 stops on a bump The stopping epoch is chosen on validation data; the test set is used once, at the end In Lab 1.3. On the plain run, a patience of 3 keeps epoch 43; a patience of 10 keeps epoch 58, with a lower loss (0.93 against 0.98).

slides.title: Four shapes cover most of what a curve can tell you
slides.text: Reading curves Four shapes cover most of what a curve can tell you What you see Likely meaning First thing to try Both losses flat at chance Rate far too low, or no signal reaches the network Overfit one batch (session 4) Loss jumps, grows or becomes "nan" Rate too high Divide the rate by 10 Training falls, validation rises Overfitting Stop earlier, more data, regularise Both fall slowly and are still falling Not finished, or rate a little low More epochs, or a rate 3 times larger

slides.text: Checkpoint What would you change first? A network with 256 hidden units trains on 400 swatches. After 60 epochs the training loss is 0.20 and still falling; the validation loss reached 0.93 at epoch 35 and is now 1.10. Which change addresses what the curves show? Raise the learning rate so that training converges faster Add a second hidden layer of 256 units Train for 60 more epochs until the training loss is near zero Keep the weights of epoch 35 and get more labelled swatches

slides.title: When training goes wrong
slides.text: Session 4 When training goes wrong Run an overfit-one-batch test and say what its result rules out Find a fault in the loss input, the learning rate and the data order Keep a debugging log that another engineer can follow 04

slides.title: A broken training script usually runs without an error
slides.text: Why this is hard A broken training script usually runs without an error Ordinary code fails loudly: an exception, a line number Training code fails quietly: a number that is worse than it should be Several faults stack, and each hides the others So you need tests with a known right answer log epoch 1 · train loss 2.130 · val loss 65.4 · val acc 0.124 log epoch 2 · train loss 2.148 · val loss 67.3 · val acc 0.126 log epoch 3 · train loss 2.149 · val loss 31.9 · val acc 0.128

slides.title: First, make the network memorise one batch
slides.text: The cheapest test First, make the network memorise one batch Take 16 examples. Train on them alone for a few hundred steps A healthy model, loss and optimiser drive the loss towards zero It takes seconds and has a known right answer It fails The fault is in the model, the loss or the update. More data will not help. It passes, and full training still fails Those three work. Look at what reaches them: the data pipeline.

slides.title: Five checks, from cheap to expensive
slides.text: The checklist Five checks, from cheap to expensive Run as found and write down the numbers: is the loss at chance, above it, "nan"? Overfit one batch Check the loss on a known case : a perfect prediction must cost about 0 Sweep the learning rate on the one-batch test, in powers of ten Test the pipeline : does every input still travel with its own label? One change at a time, and a log line for each. What you tested, what it showed, what you changed.

slides.title: A correct fix can leave the test failing
slides.text: Stacked faults A correct fix can leave the test failing State of the script One-batch loss after 300 steps Verdict As found 134.2 Fails Loss input fixed, rate still 30 4.4 Fails: another fault Loss input fixed, rate 0.1 0.08 Passes What goes wrong. Undoing a correct fix because the curve did not improve. Keep the fix when its own check passes (a perfect prediction now costs 0), and look for the next fault.

slides.title: Tag every row and see whether the pairs survive
slides.text: The data pipeline Tag every row and see whether the pairs survive tag = torch.arange(40) X = tag.float().unsqueeze(1) for xb, yb in make_batches(X, tag, 8, g): assert torch.equal( xb.squeeze(1).long(), yb) Give the pipeline inputs that are their labels Any batch where they differ is a pipeline bug Passing the one-batch test and sitting at exactly ln 8 on full data points here 2.08 → 1.23 validation loss with two fixes, and with the third (the data order), after 8 epochs (Lab 1.4)

slides.title: A loss that falls within each class and jumps at the next
slides.text: Another data-order fault A loss that falls within each class and jumps at the next batch 1 32 stripes · loss 1.98 batch 11 32 stripes · loss 0.51 batch 13 32 chevrons · loss 4.35 batch 23 32 chevrons · loss 1.37 epoch 3 val acc 0.14 · 90% of validation swatches called "dot" The swatches stored class by class and never shuffled: 87 of 94 batches hold one class From the second class on, each class starts at 2.6 to 4.3 and ends its run at 1.4 to 2.3: the network learns "say chevron", and the next class punishes it Pairs broken (Lab 1.4) look different: every batch loss stays between 2.06 and 2.12, near ln 8

slides.title: Shuffle the examples, not the batches
slides.text: The fix Shuffle the examples, not the batches Same swatches, same network, 3 epochs Classes per batch Validation accuracy Stored order, class by class 1.07 0.14 One-class batches, taken in a new order each epoch 1.07 0.22 Swatches in a new random order each epoch 7.84 0.52 The test. Print the labels of the first three batches. A representative batch looks like the whole training set: most classes, in about their usual shares.

slides.title: The usual suspects, by where they sit
slides.text: Beyond today's three The usual suspects, by where they sit Data Labels shifted or shuffled away; inputs not normalised as the model expects; the same preprocessing missing at validation. Model and loss Wrong loss input; an output layer with the wrong number of classes; a silent broadcast between (N,) and (N, 1). Update Rate too high or too low; gradients never cleared; weights frozen by mistake; evaluation mode left on.

slides.title: Where is the fault?
slides.text: Checkpoint Where is the fault? Rayan trains a classifier on ten product categories. On 16 examples the loss reaches 0.02 in 200 steps. On the full training set it stays at 2.30 for 20 epochs, at every learning rate he tries. Where should he look first? At the size of the network: it cannot hold ten categories At the data pipeline: inputs and labels no longer match At the loss function: it cannot reach zero At the learning rate: it needs a finer sweep

slides.title: The catalogue photographs are turned, shifted and in colour
slides.text: Today's data The catalogue photographs are turned, shifted and in colour 8,000 synthetic photographs, 48 by 48 pixels: 6,000 to train, 1,000 to validate, 1,000 to test. Colour says nothing about the class.

slides.title: One weight per pixel position cannot learn a pattern that moves
slides.text: Yesterday's network on today's data One weight per pixel position cannot learn a pattern that moves 0.15 validation accuracy of a two-layer network with 885,896 weights on the photographs (Lab 2.1). Chance is 0.125; on straight swatches it reached 0.79 A fully connected layer learns "bright at row 3, column 7" Shift a stripe by three pixels and every one of those weights is wrong It would need to see each pattern at every position and angle

slides.title: A convolution slides one small detector over the whole image
slides.text: Convolution A convolution slides one small detector over the whole image A kernel is a small grid of weights: 3 by 3, 5 by 5 At each position: multiply kernel and pixels under it, add up The result is a feature map: where in the image the kernel's pattern occurs The same weights at every position: a stripe is a stripe wherever it lies edge = torch.tensor([[-1., 0., 1.], [-1., 0., 1.], [-1., 0., 1.]]) out[i, j] = (img[i:i+3, j:j+3] * edge).sum() # 48 x 48 in, 46 x 46 out

slides.title: Sharing weights across positions cuts the first layer 700 times
slides.text: Why it is small Sharing weights across positions cuts the first layer 700 times Fully connected, 6,912 inputs to 128 units 884,864 Convolution, 16 kernels of 5 by 5 by 3 1,216 Whole network of Lab 2.1: three convolution blocks and a head, 25,096 weights Fewer weights to fit, and each one sees every position of every image

slides.title: Pooling shrinks the map; depth widens what a unit sees
slides.text: The rest of the network Pooling shrinks the map; depth widens what a unit sees Conv 5×5, 16 edges and bars, 48 × 48 → Pool, conv 3×3, 32 corners and crossings, 24 × 24 → Pool, conv 3×3, 64 motifs, 12 × 12 → Average, linear 64 numbers, then 8 scores Max pooling keeps the largest value of each 2 by 2 block: half the size, less sensitive to a small shift After two poolings, one unit of the third layer looks at a 20-pixel patch of the photograph The final average over all positions asks "does this motif occur?", not "where?"

slides.title: Average or flatten: count the layer that follows
slides.text: The last map and the head Average or flatten: count the layer that follows Map 32 × 6 × 6, 8 classes Inputs Head weights Average, then linear 32 264 Flatten, then linear 1,152 9,224 Count it. Flatten: inputs = channels × height × width. Average: inputs = channels. Flattened, the head holds 66% of the network's weights (5% averaged) and accepts one image size only: on a 32 × 32 swatch it fails.

slides.title: Someone has already trained the filters on a million photographs
slides.text: Pretrained backbones Someone has already trained the filters on a million photographs A backbone is a network trained on a large, general image set, published as a file of weights Early layers: edges, colours. Middle: textures, repeated shapes. Last layer: that set's own classes The early and middle layers transfer: every image task needs them In the lab: ResNet-18 11.7 million weights, 11.2 million without its 1,000-class head, trained on ImageNet-1k (1.28 million photographs, 1,000 everyday classes). A 45 MB download, loaded with one line (torchvision; the same weights are in timm).

slides.title: Remove the last layer and the network returns 512 features
slides.text: Feature extraction Remove the last layer and the network returns 512 features m = torchvision.models.resnet18( weights="IMAGENET1K_V1") m.fc = nn.Identity() # was 512 -> 1000 m.eval() with torch.no_grad(): features = m(prepare(X)) # (N, 512) The 1,000-class layer is the only part about ImageNet's classes Everything before it becomes a fixed function: photograph in, 512 numbers out Frozen : evaluation mode, no gradients, nothing trained

slides.title: Feed a backbone what it was trained on
slides.text: Preprocessing Feed a backbone what it was trained on Normalise each colour channel with the mean and standard deviation of the backbone's training set Resize towards the size it was trained at: its filters expect motifs of a certain size in pixels These numbers belong to the weights; they are published with them What goes wrong. Raw pixels in [0, 1] fed to a backbone raise no error. The features are just worse, by a little or by a lot. It is the quiet kind of fault from yesterday's list.

slides.title: Three ways to use 800 labels, from least to most trained

Partial fine-tuning Also train the last block or two. The most task-specific layers adapt; the general ones stay. Full fine-tuning Train everything at a small rate. slides.title: A frozen weight has no gradient and is never updated
slides.text: Freezing A frozen weight has no gradient and is never updated m.fc = nn.Linear(512, 8) for p in m.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False for p in m.layer4.parameters(): p.requires_grad = True for p in m.fc.parameters(): p.requires_grad = True 75% of ResNet-18's weights, without the head, sit in its last block: 8.4 of 11.2 million (Lab 2.3) "Only the last block" is still 8 million numbers fitted to 800 photographs.

slides.title: Small steps for what is already good, larger steps for what is new
slides.text: Learning rates Small steps for what is already good, larger steps for what is new optimiser = torch.optim.Adam([ {"params": m.layer4.parameters(), "lr": 3e-4}, {"params": m.fc.parameters(), "lr": 3e-3}, ]) The pretrained block starts from useful weights: it is nudged The new head starts from random numbers: it must travel One large rate for both destroys the block in the first steps

slides.title: Augmentation is extra data that costs no labels, if it keeps the label true
slides.text: Augmentation Augmentation is extra data that costs no labels, if it keeps the label true Safe for these patterns Flips, small shifts, a rotation, a change of colours: a flipped chevron is a chevron, and the class does not depend on colour. Not safe everywhere Flip a photograph of text or of a left-hand glove and the label is wrong. A heavy blur can turn a wave into a stripe. Applied to each batch in training only, with new random choices every time The validation and test photographs are never augmented

slides.text: The map for two days From text in to one token out: five stations 1 · Tokens text cut into pieces, each a number → 2 · Embeddings a vector per token, plus its position → 3 · Attention each token gathers from the others, layer after layer → 4 · Scores one number for every token of the vocabulary → 5 · Sampling one token is chosen and appended All of it must fit in the context window: the largest number of tokens the model reads at once. slides.title: A model never sees text; it sees token numbers
slides.text: Station 1 A model never sees text; it sees token numbers "A red striped rug" for Qwen2.5: 4 tokens A red striped rug The same in Arabic, سجادة مخططة حمراء: 9 tokens سجادة مخططة حمراء A tokeniser cuts text into pieces from a fixed vocabulary and returns their numbers Frequent words are one token; rare words are several pieces The tokeniser is built before training and belongs to the model

slides.title: Subword vocabularies are learnt from text by merging frequent pairs
slides.text: How the vocabulary is built Subword vocabularies are learnt from text by merging frequent pairs Start from single bytes or characters Merge the most frequent neighbouring pair into a new piece; repeat tens of thousands of times What was frequent in the training text becomes one token Anything can still be written: in the worst case, byte by byte Tokeniser in the lab Vocabulary Built from GPT-2 50,257 English web text Qwen2.5 151,665 Multilingual text multilingual-e5 250,002 About 100 languages

slides.title: The same product costs more tokens in Arabic, by a factor that depends on the tokeniser
slides.text: What the lab measured The same product costs more tokens in Arabic, by a factor that depends on the tokeniser Twelve products, each described in both languages Tokens per English word Tokens per Arabic word Arabic tokens ÷ English tokens GPT-2 (built from English) 1.54 4.71 3.14 Qwen2.5 (multilingual) 1.86 2.51 1.39 multilingual-e5 1.68 1.94 1.18 Two causes. A vocabulary with few Arabic pieces falls back to bytes, two per letter. And an Arabic word carries more: باللون is "in the colour" in one word.

slides.title: Customers do not write like the catalogue
slides.text: Beyond the catalogue Customers do not write like the catalogue The same three words Text GPT-2 e5 Qwen2.5 Catalogue Arabic سجادة مخططة حمراء 20 7 9 With short vowels سَجَّادَة مُخَطَّطَة حَمْرَاء 35 23 25 Arabizi sajjada mukhattata 7amra 11 8 12 English red striped rug 3 4 3 What goes wrong. Each short-vowel mark is a character of its own. Vowelled text is cut into single letters and marks: three times the tokens, in pieces the model has rarely seen.

slides.title: Three bills are paid in tokens
slides.text: Why you count Three bills are paid in tokens The window A model reads a limited number of tokens at once. A window of 2,048 holds about 86 English descriptions or 62 Arabic ones (Lab 3.1). The time A generating model produces one token per step. More tokens for the same sentence is more waiting. The price Hosted models charge per token read and per token written. The same content can cost more in one language.

slides.title: Each token number becomes a vector, and gets its position added
slides.text: Station 2 Each token number becomes a vector, and gets its position added The embedding table has one row per token of the vocabulary: a vector of a few hundred to a few thousand numbers The rows are weights: learnt by the same five lines as everything else A position signal is added, so that "rug" at position 4 differs from "rug" at position 1 In numbers Qwen2.5-0.5B: 151,665 rows of 896 numbers, 136 million of its 494 million weights. A small model spends a quarter of itself on the table.

slides.text: Checkpoint Why did the Arabic prompt not fit? Rayan pastes 70 product descriptions into a small model with a window of 2,048 tokens. slides.title: Attention step by step
slides.text: Session 2 Attention step by step Compute attention scores, weights and outputs for a toy sequence Apply a causal mask and say what it prevents Check an implementation against the library function 02

slides.title: A word means what its neighbours make it mean
slides.text: Station 3 A word means what its neighbours make it mean "red striped wool rug": the vector of "rug" should end up knowing its colour, pattern and material A convolution looks at fixed neighbours; text needs to reach any other position Attention lets every token collect from every other, with weights computed from the tokens themselves One sentence Attention replaces each token's vector by a weighted mean of all tokens' vectors, and learns where the weights should be large.

slides.title: Every token asks a question, offers a label and carries a content
slides.text: Three views of one token Every token asks a question, offers a label and carries a content Query What this token is looking for. Q = X @ Wq Key What this token can be found by. K = X @ Wk Value What this token hands over when it is found. V = X @ Wv Three weight matrices, learnt; the rest of attention has no weights at all The score of token i for token j is the dot product of query i and key j

slides.title: Scaled dot-product attention is four lines
slides.text: The mechanism Scaled dot-product attention is four lines S = Q @ K.T / math.sqrt(d) # 1 scores: every query against every key S = S.masked_fill(future, -inf) # 2 the causal mask (decoders only) A = torch.softmax(S, dim=-1) # 3 weights: each row adds up to 1 out = A @ V # 4 a weighted mean of the values Shapes. Five tokens with vectors of 8: Q, K and V are (5, 8), the scores and weights (5, 5), the output (5, 8) again. A layer of attention keeps the shape of what it reads.

slides.title: A decoder may look back, never ahead
slides.text: The mask A decoder may look back, never ahead red striped wool rug . red 1.00 0 0 0 0 striped 0.31 0.69 0 0 0 wool 0.15 0.09 0.75 0 0 rug 0.18 0.19 0.15 0.48 0 . 0.18 0.16 0.38 0.05 0.22 Rows: the token that looks. Columns: the token looked at Scores above the diagonal are set to minus infinity; their weights become exactly 0 In training, the token after position i is the answer for position i: it must not be visible

slides.title: Attention alone does not know the order of its tokens
slides.text: A consequence Attention alone does not know the order of its tokens Shuffle the five tokens: each token's output is unchanged, it only moves with its token (Lab 3.2) "rug red" and "red rug" would be the same to it Hence the position signal added to each embedding at station 2 Two things put order back. The position signal, and in a decoder the causal mask, which makes each output depend on what came before it.

slides.title: A transformer repeats one block many times
slides.text: From one layer to a model A transformer repeats one block many times Attention several heads side by side: tokens exchange information → Feed-forward a small two-layer network on each token by itself → Repeat 24 blocks in Qwen2.5-0.5B Heads : the vectors are split into parts that attend separately, so one token can look for several things at once Around each part: a skip connection and a normalisation, as in yesterday's ResNet, for the same reason: depth that still trains The cost of attention grows with the square of the number of tokens: one more reason windows are limited

slides.title: Encoder, decoder, or both: the mask decides what the model is for
slides.text: Three shapes of transformer Encoder, decoder, or both: the mask decides what the model is for Encoder No mask: every token sees the whole text. Output: one vector per token or per text. For classifying, tagging, embedding. This afternoon's model. Decoder Causal mask: each token sees the past. Output: scores for the next token. For generating. Tomorrow's model, and every chat assistant. Encoder-decoder An encoder reads the input; a decoder writes the output while attending to it. For translation and summarising with a fixed input.

slides.title: What does the mask protect?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does the mask protect? Zaid trains a small decoder to predict the next token of product descriptions and forgets the causal mask. The training loss falls to almost zero within one epoch. When he asks the model to write a description, it produces nonsense. Why? It memorised the training descriptions and cannot generalise It never learnt the order of the tokens in a sentence Its learning rate was too high for a model of that size In training each position could read the token it had to predict

slides.title: An embedding model turns a whole text into one vector
slides.text: Sentence embeddings An embedding model turns a whole text into one vector Text a description or a query → Encoder one vector per token → Pool the mean over the tokens → One vector 384 numbers, scaled to length 1 Trained on pairs of texts that belong together (a question and its answer, a sentence and its translation): their vectors are pulled together, others pushed apart Texts with similar meaning then lie close; you search by distance

slides.title: Cosine similarity compares directions, not lengths
slides.text: Similarity Cosine similarity compares directions, not lengths cos(a, b) = a · b / (|a| |b|): 1 for the same direction, 0 for a right angle For vectors of length 1 it is the dot product: one matrix product compares a query with every description Other measures (dot product on raw vectors, Euclidean distance) rank the same when all vectors have length 1 D = U.embed(texts, "passage: ") # (4000, 384) q = U.embed([query])[0] # (384,) sims = D @ q # (4000,) top = np.argsort(-sims)[:5]

slides.title: Read similarities as a ranking, not as a scale
slides.text: What the lab measured Read similarities as a ranking, not as a scale Compared with "a red striped rug" Cosine similarity Its Arabic translation, سجادة مخططة باللون الأحمر 0.87 An English paraphrase, "a crimson carpet with lines" 0.83 Another product, "a blue dotted shawl" 0.79 An unrelated question, "how do I return an order?" 0.78 What goes wrong. A threshold such as "similar above 0.7" copied from another model. Here everything is above 0.7; the whole ranking happens between 0.76 and 0.90.

slides.title: Brute force is exact and enough for thousands; an index trades exactness for speed
slides.text: Searching Brute force is exact and enough for thousands; an index trades exactness for speed Brute force Compare the query with every vector: one matrix product. Exact. 4,000 descriptions take well under a millisecond in NumPy. An approximate index Organise the vectors so that a query visits only some of them (FAISS is one example). Needed from millions; may miss a true neighbour, so recall must be measured again. Start exact. Measure quality with brute force first. Then an index has something to be compared with.

slides.title: Recall at 5: of what should come back, how much is in the first five?
slides.text: The measure Recall at 5: of what should come back, how much is in the first five? Rayan's team wrote 50 queries and marked the relevant descriptions of each Each query names a kind of product, a pattern and a colour: two products match, each described in both languages, so four relevant descriptions Recall at 5 = relevant found in the first five ÷ 4, averaged over the queries query red wavy table runner 1 ✓ This table runner is wavy and red. Material: camel hair. 2 ✓ Wavy table runner made of linen. Colour: red. 3 Wavy table runner made of palm fibre. Colour: orange. 4 Wool table runner with a wavy design in white.

slides.text: Checkpoint What does this recall mean? A query has four relevant descriptions. The search returns five results; two of them are relevant. A colleague says: "two out of five, so recall at 5 is 0.4". What is the right figure? 0.5: two of the four relevant descriptions were found 0.4: two of the five results are relevant 1.0: at least one relevant description is in the first five 0.8: four relevant descriptions for five places

These numbers rank the groups; they do not measure them finely.

slides.title: The search never crossed from one language to the other
slides.text: What the lab measured The search never crossed from one language to the other 100% of the top-5 results are in the query's own language 0.47 of the same-language relevant descriptions were found 0.00 of the other-language relevant descriptions were found The best other-language relevant description sits at a median rank of 1,988 of 4,000 Half of what should come back is behind a wall: recall at 5 could never pass 0.5

slides.text: Two fixes, both measured The fix that worked used a fact the catalogue already had Recall at 5 All 50 English Arabic Mixed Plain search 0.225 0.300 0.188 0.150 A: three results from the query's language, two from the other 0.210 0.300 0.150 0.150 B: after each result, add the same product's other description 0.335 0.475 0.250 0.225 Fix A asked the model to cross the wall and it could not. Fix B did not ask: the catalogue knows which two descriptions are one product.

slides.title: The remaining failures are gaps between how customers write and how the catalogue is written
slides.text: Reading the failures The remaining failures are gaps between how customers write and how the catalogue is written Query What came back Likely cause I am looking for a indigo pillow cover with a zigzag design Cushion covers with dots and triangles, other colours Synonyms: the catalogue says "chevron" and "blue" ودي بجزدان بنقاط أخضر زينة Green wall hangings, belts and blankets A dialect word for the product; only the colour matched abgha salla mu3ayyanat aswad Shawls in other patterns and colours Arabizi: Arabic in Latin letters and digits أبحث عن فاصل كتاب بنقشة النجوم لونها أحمر Star-patterned bookmarks in orange and black Wrong attribute: right product and pattern, another colour

slides.title: "Multilingual" is a claim to test on your own languages and your own text
slides.text: Multilingual models "Multilingual" is a claim to test on your own languages and your own text Quality differs by language: by how much text of it was in training, and of which kind Standard Arabic is covered far better than dialects; Arabizi and code-switching are rarer still Spelling varies between writers: hamza forms, ta marbuta, short vowels. Normalise both the catalogue and the query, then measure Report results per language; an average hides the group that is served worst Responsible use. A service that works better in one language than in another treats its users unequally. Measuring it per language is the first step, and it goes in the README.

slides.title: A language model does not write a sentence; it scores the next token
slides.text: Station 4 A language model does not write a sentence; it scores the next token Read all tokens so far, through every block → Score one number (a logit) for each of 151,936 tokens → Choose one token → Append and run the model again The last layer turns the vector at the last position into one score per token of the vocabulary A product line of 19 tokens is 19 runs of the model, each on a text one token longer Training was the same task: given real text, predict its next token. Cross-entropy loss, the five lines of Day 1

slides.title: The scores for the first token of one product line
slides.text: What the lab loads The scores for the first token of one product line Co 0.296 " 0.128 Explore 0.098 Probabilities at temperature 1, for the product "coasters, check, blue, cotton". The softmax turns scores into probabilities that add up to 1 The three most likely tokens hold about half of the probability The 200 most likely hold 0.92; the other 151,736 tokens share the rest That long, thin tail is what the sampling settings act on

slides.title: Greedy decoding takes the most likely token, every time
slides.text: The simplest choice Greedy decoding takes the most likely token, every time The same prompt gives the same text: five drafts of a product were one draft "Temperature 0" is the usual name for it Useful where a result must be repeatable: tests, extraction, the ten tasks of Lab 4.2 What the lab measured At temperature 0, 25 of 100 drafts still broke a rule: every one of them was longer than 20 words. What goes wrong. "Temperature 0, so the model is right." Greedy decoding makes an output repeatable. It does not make it correct.

slides.title: Temperature divides the scores before the softmax
slides.text: Station 5 Temperature divides the scores before the softmax z = (logits - logits.max()) / t p = np.exp(z) / np.exp(z).sum() The order of the tokens never changes Below 1 the first tokens gain; above 1 the tail gains Temperature First token Tokens holding 90% 0.2 0.981 1 0.7 0.529 8 1.0 0.296 53 1.5 0.119 126

slides.title: Nucleus sampling cuts the tail that temperature opens
slides.text: Station 5, second setting Nucleus sampling cuts the tail that temperature opens Sort the tokens; keep the most likely until their probabilities add up to top_p Drop the rest and share the probability again among those kept The two settings pull in opposite directions, and every request has a value for both, if only the default At temperature 1.5 Tokens that can be drawn First token top_p 1.0 all 0.119 top_p 0.9 126 0.132 top_p 0.5 19 0.233 Read the middle row. At a high temperature a nucleus of 0.9 still holds more than a hundred tokens. It cuts little.

slides.title: A wide tail is not creative; it is noise
slides.text: What the drafts look like A wide tail is not creative; it is noise Setting One draft for "coasters, check, blue, cotton, 35 x 150 cm" Temperature 0 Coasters, check, blue, cotton, 35 x 150 cm, perfect for a cozy summer getaway. Temperature 0.7 Coasters, a unique collection of blue blue cotton check coasters measuring 35 inches x 150 cm, perfect for adding a touch of nature to any room. Temperature 1.5 Coasters adorned in the muted blue color are coupé them beyond narrvcournoise vaccination strain elite align heading luminance Words shared by two drafts of one product: 1.00 at temperature 0, 0.20 at 0.7, 0.01 at 1.5 At 1.5, 89 of 100 drafts are no longer English only

slides.title: The instruction moved the numbers more than any sampling setting
slides.text: What the lab measured The instruction moved the numbers more than any sampling setting 100 drafts per setting Words per draft Over 20 words Not English only Break any rule Temperature 0 18.1 0.25 0.00 0.25 Temperature 0.7 19.9 0.43 0.01 0.44 Temperature 1.5 24.3 0.69 0.89 0.93 Temperature 1.5, top_p 0.5 21.5 0.52 0.05 0.56 Temperature 0.7, strict instruction 11.2 0.01 0.02 0.05 Temperature 1.5, strict instruction 21.8 0.55 0.88 0.95 Two readings. The instruction changes which tokens are likely; sampling only chooses among them. And an instruction cannot repair a distribution that temperature has flattened.

slides.text: Session 2 From base models to assistants Show what a chat template adds to a prompt Compare a base and an instruction-tuned model on the same tasks Make a base model do a task with a few-shot prompt 02

slides.title: A base model has learnt one thing: to continue text
slides.text: Where an assistant starts A base model has learnt one thing: to continue text Pretraining : predict the next token over a very large amount of text. No questions, no answers, no roles What comes out knows a great deal about language and the world as written It has no notion that a question is addressed to it TypedWrite this in capital letters: wool rug Base modelWoRlG rug Instruction-tunedWOOL RUG

slides.title: You type the same prompt; the two models do not read the same text
slides.text: What each model receives You type the same prompt; the two models do not read the same text <|im_start|>system You are Qwen, created by Alibaba Cloud. You are a helpful assistant.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user What is the capital of Saudi Arabia? Answer with one word.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant The chat template wraps your prompt in turns marked by special tokens The instruction-tuned model continues this text, and the continuation of "the assistant's turn starts here" is an answer The base model receives the bare line

slides.title: Instruction tuning is more training on conversations, with nothing added to the network
slides.text: Concept Instruction tuning is more training on conversations, with nothing added to the network Base model next-token training on text → Instruction tuning the same training, on instructions with good answers, wrapped in the template → Preference tuning pushed toward the answers people rated better Same architecture, same number of weights: only their values change The model learns the turn structure, to answer the request, and to end its turn It is the fine-tuning of Day 2, applied to a language model

slides.title: On ten small tasks the base model fails, until the prompt is written for it
slides.text: What the lab measured On ten small tasks the base model fails, until the prompt is written for it Ten tasks, temperature 0, at most 40 new tokens Right Stopped by itself Clean Instruction-tuned, plain prompt 7 of 10 9 of 10 7 of 10 Base, plain prompt 3 of 10 7 of 10 2 of 10 Base, few-shot prompt 10 of 10 0 of 10 0 of 10 Right : the expected answer is in the first line. Clean: right, stopped, one line only, so a program can use it as it is.

slides.title: A few-shot prompt is a text whose most likely continuation is the answer
slides.text: Writing for a model that continues text A few-shot prompt is a text whose most likely continuation is the answer Country: France Capital: Paris Country: Japan Capital: Tokyo Country: Saudi Arabia Capital: Two solved examples in a fixed layout, then the new case with the answer left open The examples fix the format and show what kind of answer is wanted: three tasks the instruction-tuned model missed came out right Examples help instruction-tuned models too, whenever the shape of the answer matters

slides.title: Knowing the answer and knowing when to stop are learnt separately
slides.text: The other half of an answer Knowing the answer and knowing when to stop are learnt separately prompt ends Country: Saudi Arabia / Capital: answer Riyadh runs on Country: South Korea / Capital: Seoul / Country: Thailand / Capital: Bangkok / Country: Turkey ... Generation ends when the model draws an end token, or at the limit of new tokens An instruction-tuned model learnt to end its turn; after two examples, a base model's likeliest next text is a third example The calling program sets a stop sequence or keeps the first line

slides.title: Preference tuning shapes how an assistant behaves, not what it knows
slides.text: Concept Preference tuning shapes how an assistant behaves, not what it knows People, or a model trained on their ratings, compare answers; the model is pushed toward the preferred ones This is where tone, helpfulness, refusals and "I'm sorry, but I don't have that information" come from It adds no facts: a learnt habit of declining is not knowledge of what the model knows Why it matters this afternoon In Lab 4.3 the model declines six questions it cannot know and answers two with invented facts. Both behaviours come from training, and neither is a check.

slides.title: Reasoning effort buys quality on hard tasks with tokens you pay for and wait for
slides.text: Concept Reasoning effort buys quality on hard tasks with tokens you pay for and wait for Some models write intermediate reasoning tokens before the answer; a setting says how much They are generated like any other token: one run of the model each They help on multi-step problems; a one-word extraction gains nothing In the week's numbers The small model wrote about 3 tokens a second on a laptop processor. At that speed, 300 reasoning tokens before a 19-token product line are well over a minute of waiting. Not measured here. The lab's model has no reasoning setting. Treat effort as one more column of a model-choice table: quality gained against tokens spent.

He must keep this model. What should he change? Write two solved examples, leave the new answer open, and keep the first line of the output Lower the temperature further Put "You are a helpful assistant" in front of the question Raise the limit of new tokens

slides.title: Limits: fabrication, cut-off and context
slides.text: Session 3 Limits: fabrication, cut-off and context Separate an abstention from a fabricated answer Show what a runtime does with a prompt longer than its window Write the limits of a generated output before a customer sees it 03

slides.title: The model produces a likely continuation; nothing in it checks that the text is true
slides.text: Fabrication The model produces a likely continuation; nothing in it checks that the text is true QuestionIn which year was Al-Nawl Crafts Cooperative founded, and by whom? Small modelAl-Nawl Crafts Cooperative was founded in 1998. The cooperative was established by the Al-Nawl family ... a prominent family in the textile industry of Iran. The cooperative does not exist: no model has read a word about it The answer is fluent, specific and false, and nothing in the text marks it as invented Asked in Arabic: the same year, founded by "a group of engineers in Egypt"

slides.title: Eight questions it cannot know: six declined, two answered anyway
slides.text: What the lab measured Eight questions it cannot know: six declined, two answered anyway 6 answers say "I don't have that information" 2 answers invent a year and founders 8 questions, one wording each: far too few for a rate Declining is a habit from tuning. It held for a phone number and a price, and failed for a founding year The lab's rule counts phrases: a polite refusal followed by invented "general information" passes it What goes wrong. "It refuses 75% of unanswerable questions" in a report. The lab shows that fabrication happens, not how often.

slides.title: A model's present is where its training text ended
slides.text: The cut-off A model's present is where its training text ended Asked The small model answered What is today's date? It cannot see the date, and says so Which team won the football World Cup held in 2026? It cannot "predict future events" What is the most recent year you have information about? "My last update was in 2023" Its weights were published in September 2024. The year it gives for itself is generated text, like any other answer Anything newer than the cut-off, or private, has to arrive in the prompt

slides.title: The context window counts everything: instructions, documents, question and answer
slides.text: The window The context window counts everything: instructions, documents, question and answer A fixed number of tokens the model can read at once; what is outside does not exist for it The output is written into the same window The model has a limit; the runtime is started with one too, often smaller, to save memory In the lab The runtime's window is 2,048 tokens. The shop policy and a question are 164 tokens. The policy, 110 catalogue lines and the question are about 3,400.

slides.title: A prompt that did not fit lost its beginning, and nobody was told
slides.text: What the lab measured A prompt that did not fit lost its beginning, and nobody was told Four questions on the shop policy Tokens dropped Right Answers (expected 14, 10, 300, 2) Policy, question: fits 0 4 of 4 14 days, 10 working days, 300 riyals, 2 working days Policy, long extract, question 1,402 0 of 4 60 days, 4, 1, 3 Long extract, policy, question 1,402 4 of 4 14 days, 10, 300, 2 What goes wrong. The runtime kept the end of the prompt and dropped the start, policy included. The model answered each question with a confident number.

slides.title: Count the tokens before you send, and fail loudly
slides.text: What to do about it Count the tokens before you send, and fail loudly Count Tokenise the prompt with the model's own tokeniser (Lab 3.1) and compare with the window minus the room for the answer. Refuse or shorten on purpose An error is a fault you can see. If you shorten, you choose what goes, not the runtime. Know your runtime Some return an error for a prompt that is too long; some cut silently, from the start or from the end. Test it once. A silent cut is worse than a crash. It gives a confident wrong answer that nobody can trace.

slides.title: The same policy, the same questions: 4 of 4 in English, 3 of 4 in Arabic
slides.text: Two languages The same policy, the same questions: 4 of 4 in English, 3 of 4 in Arabic Expected English Arabic 14 14 days 14 يوما 10 10 working days 10 300 300 riyals 25 ريال 2 2 working days 2 The Arabic miss is another number from the same paragraph of the policy Four questions cannot put a figure on the gap; they can tell you to measure Arabic by itself Of the two invented founding stories, one was the Arabic question Responsible use. A model that serves one language worse treats its users unequally. Per-language results go in the README, as for search.

slides.text: Before a customer reads it Write the limits down, each with what is done about it Measured limit What is done about it It invents facts it does not have It is given the product's attributes and may state nothing else It does not know the date or anything recent It is never asked about dates, prices, stock or delivery A prompt beyond the window loses its beginning Prompts are counted first; one that does not fit is refused Arabic answers were wrong more often Arabic output gets its own test set And say what it is. A draft written by a language model, read by the shop team before it is published.

slides.title: Where did "60 days" come from?
slides.text: Checkpoint Where did "60 days" come from? A script sends the shop policy, then 110 catalogue lines, then a question on returns, about 3,400 tokens in all, to a runtime with a window of 2,048 at temperature 0. The answer is "60 days"; the policy says 14. What happened? The policy was written after the model's training cut-off The sampling settings let an unlikely token through The runtime dropped the start of the prompt, the policy with it, and the model answered without it The model cannot read numbers reliably in a long text

slides.title: The family follows from what goes in and what must come out
slides.text: Model families The family follows from what goes in and what must come out Family Reads Produces This week Convolutional network An image A class or a feature vector Naqsh: ResNet-18, 11.7 million weights Encoder A text One vector, or a label Khayt: multilingual-e5-small, 118 million Decoder A text The next token, again and again Wasf: Qwen2.5-0.5B, 494 million Diffusion model Noise and a text An image Not used Vision-language model Images and text Text Shortlisted for Naqsh, not measured Start from the task, not from the newest model. A search needs vectors; a classifier needs a label; only drafting needs generation.

slides.title: A diffusion model makes an image by removing noise, step by step
slides.text: Concept A diffusion model makes an image by removing noise, step by step Start an image of pure noise → Denoise a network predicts the noise; a little is removed → Repeat tens of steps, each guided by the text → Image a new picture that matches the text Trained on images with added noise: the task is to predict the noise, a regression loss One image costs many runs of the network, as one sentence costs many runs of a decoder For the cooperative: catalogue illustrations, never a photograph of a product that exists

slides.title: A vision-language model turns image patches into tokens a decoder can read
slides.text: Concept A vision-language model turns image patches into tokens a decoder can read An image encoder cuts the picture into patches and gives a vector per patch The vectors enter the language model beside the text tokens; attention does the rest Image encoders of this kind are trained on pictures with their captions: matching pairs pulled together, as for yesterday's sentence embeddings For Naqsh A hosted vision-language model could be asked "which pattern is this?" with no training at all. Nobody has measured it on the cooperative's photographs, and the photographs would leave the shop's server.

slides.title: Open-weight or hosted: who runs it, and where the data goes
slides.text: Where the model runs Open-weight or hosted: who runs it, and where the data goes Open-weight, on your server You download the weights and run them. The data stays. The version never changes unless you change it. You pay for the machine and the work of running it, and the licence is yours to read. Hosted, behind an interface The provider runs it. Much larger models than your server holds. You pay per token. The text or image leaves your server, and the provider updates and retires versions on its own calendar. In the case. Anything that leaves the shop's server needs the sign-off of Bushra Al-Aqeel, the data protection officer, before a single test request.

slides.title: Size and latency span four orders of magnitude across the three models
slides.text: What the week measured Size and latency span four orders of magnitude across the three models One request on a laptop processor File Latency Small convolutional network (Lab 2.1) 0.1 MB 1.9 ms ResNet-18, one photograph 45 MB 35 ms multilingual-e5-small, one query and the search 470 MB 39 ms Qwen2.5-0.5B, one product line of 19 tokens 990 MB 6,500 ms An encoder runs once per request; a decoder runs once per token written A latency budget belongs to the use: a person waiting for a search, or a batch of 2,000 drafts overnight

slides.title: Read the licence of each size, and ask what the model was trained on
slides.text: May we use it? Read the licence of each size, and ask what the model was trained on Model Licence of the weights For a shop multilingual-e5-small MIT Yes Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct Apache 2.0 Yes Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct A research licence of its own No ResNet-18, ImageNet weights BSD 3-Clause Sign-off: trained on ImageNet, whose terms of access name non-commercial research and education What goes wrong. "Same family, same licence." One size of a family can carry other terms than its smaller and larger siblings.

slides.title: Screen first, compare second, then write two lines
slides.text: The method Screen first, compare second, then write two lines 1 · Screen licence, data leaving the server, size, measured at all, inside the latency budget → 2 · Compare quality against the simpler alternative, latency, size, cost → 3 · Justify "because": the numbers that decide. "But": the risk, and who signs A model that may not be used cannot be chosen, so quality comes after the screen "Not measured" removes an option from this week's table. It is not a verdict on the model Cost: a model on your own server adds nothing per request; a hosted one is paid per token

Test results Per class or per language, on a test you can call fair, with three failures and a likely cause each. The simpler alternative The same test for both. The difference in items as well as in points. Latency and size Median time of one request on a laptop processor, and the size of the model file. Licences and limits The licence and provenance of every model and dataset, with its address, and the limits written for the person who reads the output.
